title: Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa: The Crown and the Wilderness
body:
Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa: The Crown and the Wilderness

Festive Preparations

Twelve years passed in Ayodhyā, and they were the best years the kingdom had ever known.

Rāma and Sītā lived in a happiness so complete that it seemed to warm the whole city. They were young, and they loved one another with a love that had recognition at its root, and they moved through the palace and the capital as a blessing moves, leaving people gladder for having seen them. Rāma had grown from the boy who broke the bow into a man in the fullness of his powers, and every quality that had shown early in him had deepened. He was just, and he was merciful, and he was accessible; the humblest citizen could bring him a grievance and be heard with the same grave attention he gave to a minister. He forgot no one’s name. He remembered the troubles of ordinary people and asked after them. The love the city had felt for the infant prince had grown, over these twelve years, into something closer to worship, and it was not the worship of fear or distance but of gratitude. The people of Ayodhyā simply could not imagine a better man to one day be their king, and they thought of that day, when it should come, with pure anticipation.

For Dasharatha was growing old. He had been old already when Rāma was born, and now the years had gathered on him, and though he still ruled well and his mind was clear, his body was telling him what bodies tell all of us in the end. And one morning it told him plainly.

He was at his mirror, or being attended by his barber, the tellers vary, when he saw it: a single grey hair, there by his ear, catching the light. One white thread among the dark. And Dasharatha, who had faced demons and armies without flinching, looked at that one grey hair and felt his own mortality settle onto him like a cold hand.

We should not pass over this too quickly, for it is one of the truest small moments in the whole story, and every one of us will have our own version of it if we have not had it already. It is not the great catastrophes that tell us we are mortal; those we half expect. It is the small ordinary sign, the grey hair, the stiffness in the morning, the name that will not come to the tongue, the stair that is harder than it used to be. In such a trifling thing the whole enormous fact of our passing suddenly stands revealed, and we understand, not as an idea but in the body, that our time is finite and running out, and that whatever we mean to do with our life we had better be about it. Dasharatha looked at one white hair and heard, quite clearly, the messenger of his own ending, and he resolved to act while there was still time to act.

He would crown Rāma. He would install his beloved eldest son as Yuvarāja, the prince-regent, the heir apparent, and see with his own living eyes the thing he most wanted to see in all the world: Rāma seated in power, the kingdom safe in those good hands, before his own eyes should close for the last time. It was the natural, the right, the joyful decision of an old king at the end of a long reign, and he made it with a full and happy heart.

He summoned his council and the elders of the city and the representatives of the people, and he put it to them, though it was hardly in doubt. He spoke of his age, and of his long reign, and of his wish to lay down his burden into worthy hands while he yet lived. And then he named Rāma, and asked their will.

The assembly did not merely consent. It erupted. The proposal was met with a joy so immediate and so total that it swept the hall, the ministers, the elders, the citizens’ representatives, all of them acclaiming the choice with one voice, as though the king had offered them the thing they had most secretly longed for and never dared to ask. Was there any objection, the old king asked, half- teasing, knowing the answer, was there any among them who did not wish to see Rāma crowned? And they laughed and shouted their love, and told him that the only complaint the people of Ayodhyā could possibly have was that they had waited this long, and that they wished the coronation might be tomorrow.

Dasharatha’s heart overflowed. Here was the perfect close to a long life: his kingdom and his own dearest wish in perfect accord, his people begging for the very thing he most desired to give them. He gave orders that the coronation should indeed be held at once, the very next day, before any inauspicious delay could creep in. Let the sacred vessels be gathered, he said, the waters of the holy rivers brought, the whole city decked and lit; let Rāma keep the night’s vigil with Sītā as the rite required; and let Ayodhyā wake tomorrow to crown the prince it loved.

And the city threw itself into the preparations with a gladness that lit the night. Garlands were strung across every street until the air was heavy with the scent of flowers. Banners rose on every rooftop. The great ceremonial ways were swept and watered and spread with fresh sand; lamps were made ready in their thousands; musicians tuned their instruments; the whole capital, high and low, rich and poor, gave itself over to a single shared and mounting joy. Tomorrow their Rāma would be crowned. There had never been such a night in Ayodhyā, so bright with lamps, so loud with happiness, so certain of its coming morning.

And here we must pause, because the story is about to turn, and it turns exactly here, at the very summit of the joy. Everything is ready. Everyone is happy. The old king has his wish, the people have theirs, the good prince is about to receive the crown that everyone on earth agrees he deserves. Nothing could seem more settled, more certain, more sure to arrive. If you did not know the story, you would expect the next chapter to be the coronation and the happy ending.

It is one of the deep truths this epic keeps returning to: that our lives can be brightest in the very hour before the darkness, that fate does its cruelest work not in the depths but at the heights, and that the distance between the summit of our happiness and the beginning of our sorrow can be a single night, a single whisper, a single bitter heart in a dark room while the rest of the city sings. Ayodhyā blazed with lamps and rang with joy, and no one in all that happy city knew that in one small chamber, away from the light, the whole bright future was already being unmade, word by poisonous word.

For while Ayodhyā prepared to crown its prince, a hunchbacked maidservant was climbing the stairs to her mistress’s rooms, carrying in her twisted heart the ruin of them all.

Manthara’s Evil Counsel

Her name was Manthara, and she was the hunchbacked maidservant of Queen Kaikeyī, and she had come with Kaikeyī from her father’s kingdom long ago and served her all these years. She loved her mistress, in her way, with the fierce narrow possessive love of one who has nothing else, and she loved Kaikeyī’s son Bharata as though he were her own. And that love, twisted through her twisted frame and her sour lonely heart, was about to become the instrument of a catastrophe.

She was on the palace roof when she saw the city being decked, and she asked what the celebration was for, and someone told her: tomorrow Rāma is to be crowned Yuvarāja. And where the whole rest of Ayodhyā heard that news with joy, Manthara heard it and went cold, and then hot, and something in her that had perhaps been waiting years for its moment woke and uncoiled.

She went to Kaikeyī’s chamber. And she found the queen exactly as anyone who knew Kaikeyī would have expected to find her: happy. For this is the thing that must be understood first, before anything else, and understood clearly, because everything that follows is a tragedy and not a simple tale of a wicked woman. Kaikeyī was not wicked. Kaikeyī loved Rāma. She loved him truly, and more than that, the tellers are careful to say, she may have loved him even beyond her own son Bharata. Rāma had always been especially dear to her; he had a particular tenderness for this stepmother; the bond between them was real and warm. When Manthara came in, Kaikeyī was glad at the news of the coronation, glad with an open heart, and she even took a jewel from her own person and offered it to Manthara as one shares a gift in a happy hour, saying in effect: is this not wonderful news, our Rāma to be crowned?

And Manthara refused the jewel, and let it fall, and began her work.

What follows is one of the most chillingly observed passages in all the epic, because it is not a tale of a spell or a poison or a supernatural corruption. It is simply a portrait of how a good mind is poisoned by patient, malicious speech, and it is terrifyingly true to life. Manthara did not shout. She did not accuse. She began softly, with a false grief, a heavy sigh, a show of pitying her mistress, and Kaikeyī, puzzled, asked her what was wrong, and so the hook was set, for Kaikeyī herself now asked to hear the poison.

Foolish woman, Manthara said in effect, to rejoice at your own ruin. Do you not see what this means? While you smile, they are settling your doom. Once Rāma is crowned, it is Kausalyā, his mother, who becomes the great queen, the queen-mother, first in all honour. And what will you be then? A lesser wife in a rival’s house. Kausalyā has waited years for this hour, and when it comes she will remember every slight, real or imagined, and you will be made to pay for having been the favourite. You will serve her. Your Bharata, who has as much right to the throne as Rāma, will be nothing, a shadow at another man’s court, and if he is lucky he will be sent far away, and if he is unlucky, he will not be suffered to live at all, for what king was ever safe while a rival brother breathed? You are not watching a coronation, my queen. You are watching the beginning of your own slavery and your son’s destruction, and you are smiling at it.

Now every word of this was false, and we know it is false, and the story is at pains to show us that it is false. Rāma loved Bharata as his own breath; Bharata loved Rāma the same; there was not the smallest danger to Bharata from Rāma’s crowning, and Kaikeyī, in her right mind, knew it. She said so, at first. She resisted. She told Manthara she was talking nonsense, that Rāma was as dear to her as Bharata, that Rāma would never harm his brother, that she was glad and would stay glad. She pushed the poison away.

But Manthara did not stop. This is the terrible patience of the thing. She had the whole night, and she used it. Again and again she returned to the wound, pressing, twisting, painting the picture darker each time, summoning up every buried fear a second wife and a mother might carry, magnifying every shadow, until slowly, slowly, the steady drip of it began to wear through Kaikeyī’s certainty. A jealous fear once spoken cannot easily be unheard. The mind returns to it. And Kaikeyī, lying in the dark with Manthara’s whispers coiling around her, began, against her own better nature, to be afraid. What if it were true? What if she were being a fool? What if her love for Rāma were blinding her to her son’s danger? The love did not vanish, but the fear grew up alongside it and began to choke it, the way a weed chokes a flower not by killing it directly but by taking its light and its air.

Let us name plainly what is happening here, because it is a warning every one of us needs. Jealousy is a fire, and the terrible thing about it is that it consumes first the vessel that holds it. Kaikeyī was a good woman with a real love in her heart, and that love was being turned, drop by poisonous drop, into its opposite, not by any fault in Rāma, who had done nothing but be worthy of a crown, but by the persistent whispering of a bitter soul who could not bear another’s joy. And it worked because the poison was mixed with just enough of something real, a mother’s fear for her son, a wife’s fear of being displaced, fears that were not wicked in themselves and could be twisted precisely because they were natural. The most dangerous lies are the ones wrapped around a splinter of truth. Manthara did not have to invent Kaikeyī’s love for Bharata; it was real; she only had to convince the mother that the love was in danger, and a mother frightened for her child will do things no argument could ever have moved her to.

By the deep of the night, the change was complete. The Kaikeyī who had offered a jewel in gladness at the news of Rāma’s crowning was gone, and in her place sat a woman rigid with a fear that had hardened into resolve. She would not let it happen. She would save her son. She would save herself. And Manthara, seeing that her long night’s work had taken hold, moved now to the second and colder part of her design, for it was not enough to make Kaikeyī afraid; she had to give the fear a weapon. And Kaikeyī, as it happened, held such a weapon in her hand, and had held it for years without ever meaning to use it.

For long ago, on a battlefield of the gods, Kaikeyī had saved Dasharatha’s life, and the grateful king had granted her two boons, any two things she might ever ask, to be claimed whenever she wished. She had never claimed them. She had had no need. They had sat unused all these years, a forgotten kindness, a sleeping debt.

Manthara now woke that sleeping debt and put it into her mistress’s hand like a blade. Use the boons, she urged. Go to the king. Ask for two things, and hold him to his word, for a king cannot break a granted boon and keep his honour. Ask first that Bharata be crowned in Rāma’s place. And ask second, so that Rāma cannot remain to threaten your son, that Rāma be sent away into the Daṇḍaka forest, into exile, for fourteen years. Fourteen years in the wilderness, and Bharata’s throne secure long before he returns, if he returns at all. This is how you save your son. This is the only way.

And Kaikeyī, no longer herself, listened to the whole monstrous plan and did not recoil from it. She took it in. She agreed to it. And she rose, and cast off her fine garments, and let down her hair, and went to the sulking-room, the chamber where a queen goes to show her displeasure, and threw herself down on the bare floor in soiled clothes to wait for the king, with two demands ready on her lips that would shatter a kingdom, break an old man’s heart, and send the best of men into the wilderness. The lamps of Ayodhyā still blazed outside, and the city still sang, still certain of its happy morning. It did not know that its morning had already been murdered in a dark room by a whisper.

Kaikeyī Succumbs

Dasharatha came to Kaikeyī’s apartments that night in the best mood of his long life. Of all his queens she had always been the one whose company most lifted him, the one whose rooms he sought when he wished simply to be happy, and on this night of all nights, with the coronation of his beloved son arranged for the morning and the whole city singing outside, he came to share his joy with the wife who had always known best how to share it. He came expecting light, and music, and Kaikeyī bright and glad to meet him.

He found darkness.

The chamber was unlit. And when his eyes adjusted he saw, with a shock that stopped him in the doorway, his queen lying on the bare floor, her jewels cast aside, her hair unbound and disordered, her fine clothes exchanged for the soiled garments of mourning. This was the kopa-griha, the sulking-room, and its meaning was unmistakable: a queen displayed herself so only in the extremity of grief or anger, to compel a husband’s attention to some wound. Dasharatha’s happiness turned to alarm in a heartbeat. That Kaikeyī, his Kaikeyī, of all of them the least given to sulks and scenes, should be lying so on this night of all nights, filled him with a bewildered dread.

He went to her at once, and knelt, and gathered her up, all tenderness and fear. What was this? Who had wronged her? Was she ill? Had someone offended her? Only name it, he said, and it would be set right; there was nothing in his power he would not do to lift this grief from her; let her only tell him what she wished and it was hers. He heaped reassurances on her, this doting old husband, promising the earth to comfort the wife he loved best, entirely unaware that he was, with every fond word, tightening the noose around his own neck.

For Kaikeyī let him make his promises, and then she asked him to make them binding. She would tell him her wish, she said, but first he must swear. He must swear by all that a king holds sacred, by his own truth, by the honour of the house of Ikshvāku, that he would grant what she asked, whatever it might be, without refusing. Bind yourself, she said. Give me your oath, and then you shall hear it.

And Dasharatha, besotted, suspecting nothing, laughing almost at her earnestness, swore. He swore the great oath. He called his own truth and his lineage and his gods to witness that whatever Kaikeyī asked, he would perform it, and that he would sooner die than break his word to her. He gave her, freely and completely, the one thing that would leave him no way out. And having sworn, he asked her, gently, what she wished.

Then Kaikeyī rose, and the woman who spoke was not the woman Dasharatha had loved for all those years. Her voice was cold and level and certain. She reminded him of the old battlefield, and the two boons he had granted her and she had never claimed. Now, she said, she would claim them, and he was bound by his oath just now sworn to grant them, and she named them.

The first: that Bharata, her son, should be crowned Yuvarāja in the morning, in the place prepared for Rāma.

The second: that Rāma should be sent that same day into the Daṇḍaka forest, clad in bark, to live as an ascetic for fourteen years.

For a moment Dasharatha did not understand. The words were too monstrous to land all at once. He asked her, surely, to repeat them, or perhaps he simply stared, his mind refusing the sense of what his ears had taken in. And then it reached him, the whole shape of it, and it struck him down as no weapon on any battlefield ever had. He fell. The tellers say he collapsed as a great tree falls, all at once, the strength going out of him, and lay stunned on the floor of the chamber where he had come to be happy, and could not speak, and could not rise.

Let us stop and see clearly what has been done here, because the horror of it is precise and worth understanding. Kaikeyī has not asked for a crime exactly. She has asked for two things that are, in the bare letter, within a king’s power to grant, the coronation of one son, the sending-away of another, and she has secured them by the one mechanism a man of honour cannot escape: his own given word. That is the trap’s cruel elegance. Dasharatha could refuse a demand backed by force; he could argue against a demand backed by mere will; but a demand backed by his own sacred oath, freely sworn moments before, he cannot refuse without destroying the very thing that makes him who he is. To break the oath is to become a king whose word is worthless, to poison the well of truth on which his whole kingdom and his whole honour rest. Kaikeyī, or rather the poison speaking through Kaikeyī, has weaponized his virtue against him. His greatest strength, his absolute fidelity to his word, has been turned into the instrument of his destruction. There is no crueler trap than the one built out of a good man’s own goodness.

And there is a further cruelty in it, quieter and sadder. The old king, lying broken on the floor, understood that the wife he had trusted above all others had planned this, had lain in wait for him in the dark with this ready, had let him pour out his love and make his fond promises knowing all the while what she would ask. The betrayal was not only of his kingdom and his son but of the intimate trust of decades, and it went into him like a cold blade. The Kaikeyī he had loved was, as far as he could tell, simply gone, and a stranger with her face sat over him demanding the ruin of everything he held dear.

When he could speak, he did not command; he had no ground to command, for he had sworn. He pleaded. He begged. This too is part of the terrible scene, that a great king was reduced to weeping at his wife’s feet, offering her anything, everything, if only she would release him from these two demands. Ask for the whole earth for Bharata, he said in effect, ask for treasure without limit, ask for anything under heaven, but not this, not the exile of Rāma, not the breaking of my heart and my kingdom. He wept and he clutched at her and he abased himself utterly, an old man destroyed, and it moved her not at all.

For Kaikeyī had made herself cold, and she turned his own honour back upon him with every plea. A king’s word cannot be broken, she said. You have sworn. If you refuse me now, you are forsworn before your court and your gods, and the house of Ikshvāku, which has never in all its generations broken a promise, is disgraced forever through you. Would you save your son and damn your honour? Would you have it said that Dasharatha lied? She held his virtue up before him like a mirror and made it a cage. He had built his whole life on the sanctity of his given word, and she used that against him with a precision that was almost surgical, so that the more he loved his honour the more surely he was bound to destroy his heart.

The night wore on toward morning, the lamps of the coronation still burning across the city, the people still asleep in their happy certainty, and in the dark chamber the old king lay broken between two impossible things: his love for his son and his fidelity to his word, and Kaikeyī immovable above him insisting he could not keep both. He wept until he had no more strength to weep. He pleaded until pleading was plainly useless. And still the demands stood, unwithdrawn, unwithdrawable, waiting for the daylight that would make them real.

He was still lying there, unmanned, unmoving, when the first grey of the dreadful morning began to show, and with it came the sounds of the city stirring toward the celebration that would never happen, and the knowledge that soon, very soon, someone would have to send for Rāma.

Wife or Demon?

The night would not release him. Dasharatha lay on the floor of the dark chamber where he had come to be happy, and the hours crawled by, and the demands did not soften, and slowly, as a man drowning in slow water understands at last that no one is coming, the old king began to grasp that this was real, that it would not be taken back, that the morning was coming and would make it true.

He passed through every stage a broken man passes through. First there had been disbelief, the mind simply refusing the words. Then there had been pleading, the frantic offering of everything else, the whole earth for Bharata, treasure without measure, anything, anything but this. And when the pleading struck the cold wall of Kaikeyī’s resolve and fell back useless, he passed into something worse, into a grief so total that it took the shape almost of madness, and he wept and raved and clutched at her feet and at his own breast, and called on the dawn not to come, and it did him no good at all.

And then, when grief had exhausted itself, came anger, and for the first time in all the years of their marriage Dasharatha looked at Kaikeyī with something other than love. He saw her now as though for the first time, this cold implacable creature sitting above his ruin, and he did not know her. Where was the woman he had cherished? Where was the wife whose company had been the joy of his old age, who had loved his son Rāma with an open heart only yesterday? The thing that sat before him now, unmoved by his tears, weaponizing his own honour against him, deaf to every appeal of love or pity, seemed to him no wife at all.

Are you a woman, he cried out to her at last, or are you some demon sent to destroy my house? For no woman, no human wife, could do this thing. What creature but a rākshasī, a she-demon out of the pit, could sit unmoved while an old man wept at her feet and beg for nothing but the ruin of the best and gentlest of sons? He had shared his throne with her, his bed, his whole heart; he had denied her nothing in all their years; and she had waited, patient as a serpent, for the one night when she could strike the blow that would kill him and destroy his line and cast his beloved son into the wilderness. This was not the act of a wife. It was the act of an enemy who had lived in his house wearing a wife’s face.

Let us pause on that terrible question, wife or demon, because the story means us to sit with it, and because the honest answer is more disturbing than either simple choice. Kaikeyī was not, in truth, a demon. She was a woman, a good woman once, who had been poisoned. And that is the more frightening truth, for a demon is a thing apart, a horror we can hold at arm’s length, but a good soul turned to this by nothing more than jealous fear and a bitter whisper, that is a horror that lives close to home, that could visit any house, that reminds us how thin the wall is between the love that would give everything and the fear that would destroy everything, and how quickly one can be turned into the other by the patient dripping of poison into a frightened heart. Dasharatha called her a demon because he could not bear the truer thing: that the wife he loved had really done this, as herself, with her own will, having been made capable of it by an evil that worked not from outside her but from within, through her own real fears turned against her.

And Kaikeyī heard herself called a demon, and it did not move her, and that failure to be moved is itself the measure of how deep the poison had gone. She answered him, and her answers were all of one kind: she threw his own virtue back in his face. You gave your word, she said. You swore the great oath. The house of Ikshvāku has never broken a promise in all its generations. Will you be the first? Will you have it said forever that Dasharatha lied, that his word was smoke, that a king of the Solar Line broke faith to spare himself a grief? She did not argue that the exile was just. She did not need to. She had only to remind him, again and again, remorselessly, that he was bound, that his honour was the chain, that to save his son he must become the one thing he had spent his whole life refusing to be: a man forsworn.

It was a devil’s logic and it was airtight, and the old king had no answer to it, because in a terrible way it was true. He had built his life on the sanctity of the given word. His people trusted him because his word was iron. His whole moral world rested on the principle that a king does not lie, that a promise is a promise though it cost the promiser everything. And now that very principle, the foundation of all his honour, had become the trap that would force him to destroy his own heart. If he broke his word, he betrayed everything he was. If he kept it, he betrayed everyone he loved. There was no third road. Kaikeyī had built a cage out of his own goodness, and every bar of it was something he himself believed in, and so he could not break a single one.

He raged, and he wept, and he cursed her, and he cursed the hour he had granted the boons, and he cursed the fate that had brought him to this, and none of it changed anything. The demands stood. His oath stood. And the daylight came anyway, grey and pitiless, as daylight does, indifferent to the ruin it was about to expose.

The old king lay spent. He had no more anger and no more tears. He understood now, in the grey light, that he was going to lose his son, and that he was going to lose him by his own hand, through his own honoured word, and that there was nothing, nothing at all, that he could do to prevent it. The knowledge hollowed him out. Whatever had been strong in him, the warrior who fought beside the gods, the king who ruled a golden age, was gone, and what was left was only a heartbroken old man who could not even rise from the floor, who could not bear to give the order that must be given, and who lay in the growing light dreading the moment when someone would have to send for Rāma and tell him what his father’s oath had done to him.

He could not do it. He had not the strength even to speak the words. And so it fell to Kaikeyī, cold and efficient to the end, to send for Rāma herself, to summon the son to the chamber where the father lay broken, so that she could deliver with her own mouth the decree that the father had no strength left to speak. She gave the order. A servant went. And somewhere across the waking palace, in the rooms where he had spent the night in the sacred vigil of one about to be crowned, Rāma received the summons to attend his father, and rose, and came, expecting, perhaps, that this was the beginning of his coronation, and walked toward the darkened chamber where the worst news of his life was waiting.

Behold a Wonder!

Rāma came to the chamber expecting joy and found catastrophe.

He had risen that morning from the vigil of one about to be crowned, purified, fasting, his mind turned toward the great responsibility he was to take up. When the summons came to attend his father, he thought nothing strange in it; the coronation was that very day; of course the king would wish to see him. He came, as he always came to his father, with love and with reverence, ready to kneel and receive a blessing.

He crossed the threshold and stopped.

The room was dark and disordered. His father, the great king, the conqueror, the mighty Dasharatha, lay collapsed and weeping upon the floor, unable to rise, unable even to look up, so unmanned by grief that he could not speak his son’s name. And beside him stood Kaikeyī, upright, cold, dry-eyed, with a face Rāma had never seen her wear. In an instant Rāma understood that something terrible had happened, though he could not yet guess what. His first thought, his only thought, was for his father. He went to him at once, all alarm and tenderness, kneeling beside the broken old man, taking his hand, asking what was wrong, who had wounded him, how he might set it right. Had he, Rāma, given some offence? Only let him know the cause of his father’s grief and he would spend his life to cure it.

But Dasharatha could not answer. He could only weep, and turn his face away, and clutch his son’s hand, and be unable to say the thing that had to be said. The sight of Rāma, come in innocence and love, expecting a crown, about to be told of his exile, was more than the old king could bear, and he broke down entirely and could not speak a word.

So Rāma turned to Kaikeyī, whom he trusted, whom he loved as a second mother, and asked her what had happened to his father, and begged her to tell him plainly, whatever it was.

And Kaikeyī told him. Coldly, completely, sparing nothing, she laid out the whole of it: the two boons, long ago granted; her claiming of them now; the king bound by his oath and unable to refuse. Bharata was to be crowned in Rāma’s place. And Rāma himself was to go that very day into the Daṇḍaka forest, in the bark garments of an ascetic, to live in exile for fourteen years. The king could not bring himself to speak these commands, she said, because he was weak with grief; but the commands were given, and bound by the royal word, and Rāma, if he was the son of truth he claimed to be, would honour them.

There was a silence in the chamber.

And then Rāma did the thing that is the whole heart of this chapter, the thing that gives it its name, for it was a wonder, and the tellers have marvelled at it ever since. He did not rage. He did not weep. He did not so much as change countenance. He heard the sentence that turned his crown into exile, that took from him in a single morning the kingdom, the throne, the honour, the whole bright future that had been his an hour before, and he received it with perfect, unshaken calm, as serenely as if she had told him some small ordinary thing.

Is that all, he said in effect. Then it is easily done. If my father has given his word, his word must be kept, and I am glad to be the means of keeping it. A son’s first duty is to preserve his father’s honour and to make his father’s word true. If my going to the forest for fourteen years is the price of my father’s truth, then I go gladly, and count it no hardship but a privilege. Let Bharata be crowned; he is worthy, and I shall be glad to see it. Send word to the forest and I will leave today.

Let us stop and understand what we are seeing, because it is easy to read this calm as coldness and it is the opposite of coldness. Rāma was not a man without feeling; he loved the world he was losing as much as any man could. Nor was his calm a matter of not yet understanding; he understood completely, at once, all that was being taken from him. His serenity came from somewhere deeper than feeling and deeper than shock. It came from a settled conviction, held so far down in him that it had become the very floor he stood on, that duty is the one thing a man truly possesses, the one thing that cannot be taken from him, because it is the one thing he can choose to give. They could take his crown. They could take his kingdom. They could send him into the wilderness. But whether he met that loss with honour or with bitterness, whether he kept faith with his father’s word or broke under the injustice of it, that was his alone to decide, and no boon and no queen and no cruelty could touch it. In the very moment of his greatest loss, Rāma reached for the one thing no one could take, and held it, and was free.

This is the secret of his calm, and it is worth carrying out of this chamber into our own smaller trials. When everything is taken from us, one thing remains: how we bear it. That remaining thing is small, and it is everything. Rāma knew it, and stood on it, and so the sentence that would have destroyed a lesser man left him untouched in the only place that finally matters.

And so, having accepted his exile without a murmur, Rāma turned his whole attention to the one being in that room who was suffering more than he was: his father. For the old king was destroyed, and Rāma’s calm, far from wounding him, only deepened his agony, because it showed him the full measure of the son he was losing. Rāma knelt again beside Dasharatha and gave himself entirely to consoling him. Do not grieve, father, he said gently. You have done no wrong. You have kept your word, and that is your glory, not your shame. I am not being punished; I am being given the chance to serve your truth. Fourteen years is not long. I will keep my discipline in the forest and return to you, and these years will pass like a dream, and you must not let this grief consume you. Be at peace. Your honour is safe, and your son is content, and there is nothing here to weep for.

He comforted the man whose oath had ruined him. He soothed the author of his exile. He asked nothing for himself, expressed no reproach, sought no comfort, but poured out his whole strength in the effort to ease his father’s pain. And the old king clung to him and wept the harder, because every gentle word showed him more clearly the goodness he was casting away, and because he understood now, past all doubt, that the son he was losing was better than any crown, better than any kingdom, better by far than the wretched honour that was forcing him to let him go.

That was the wonder of that dark morning: not that a prince lost a kingdom, for kingdoms are lost every age, but that a man could lose everything in an hour and stand so completely unshaken, and turn from his own ruin to comfort the one who had ruined him. Ayodhyā would remember that morning forever, and would tell it forever, not as the story of an injustice, though it was one, but as the first great showing of what manner of man their Rāma was, and why the love they bore him was not misplaced.

Storm and Calm

The news went out from the chamber like a crack running through ice, and where it reached, it broke hearts. But it did not break them all the same way, and in the different ways that different people met this disaster, the story shows us their souls.

It reached Kausalyā, Rāma’s own mother, and it felled her. She had waited a lifetime to see this day, the day her son was crowned, the day her long patience as the senior but not the best-loved queen was at last rewarded; and now, in a single morning, the coronation had become an exile, and her only son was to be taken from her for fourteen years, torn away into a wilderness of beasts and demons. She collapsed under the weight of it. When Rāma came to her, she clung to him and wept as though her heart would tear loose, and she said the thing that every mother in her place would say: if you must go, take me with you. Let me follow you as your shadow. I cannot live here without you; the palace will be a tomb; how can a mother stay behind in comfort while her child sleeps on the forest floor? Let me come, or let me die.

And Rāma had to console her too, gently, firmly, as he had consoled his father, but with a different argument, for her duty was different. Your place is here, mother, he told her. My father is broken; if you leave him now, in his grief, you will destroy him, and a wife’s first duty is to stand by her husband in his darkest hour. And there is the court to guide, and the kingdom to steady, in this time of confusion. To follow me would be to abandon the very duties that are yours. Stay, and be strong, and hold this house together until I return. Fourteen years will pass, and I will come back to your arms. Your grief is love, and I honour it, but let it not pull you from your dharma. And by such words, slowly, he steadied her, anchoring her breaking heart to the one thing that could hold it, the quiet duty that remained to her.

But if grief was the storm in Kausalyā, in Lakshmaṇa it was fire.

Lakshmaṇa heard the news and did not weep. He blazed. All the fierce protective love that had bound him to Rāma since the cradle rose up in him now as a towering, shaking rage, and it was terrible to see, for Lakshmaṇa was a warrior of tremendous power and his fury was not an idle thing. This was injustice, naked and monstrous, and every fibre of him rebelled against submitting to it. He came to Rāma with his whole being trembling, and the words poured out of him hot and reckless. What madness is this, he demanded. That a doting old king, besotted by a scheming wife, should throw away the rightful heir on the strength of some ancient rash promise extracted from him in a weak moment? This is not dharma; this is dotage; this is a kingdom handed to injustice because one bitter woman willed it. Why should we submit to it? Why should the best of men go into the wilderness so that intrigue may sit on the throne? Give me the word, brother, only the word, and I will set this right. Let the old king keep his forest decree; I will guard your coronation with my bow, and any man, any faction, any power that stands against your rightful crowning will answer to me. If the whole court and the king himself resist, then let them; I do not fear them; I will make you king today over the objections of them all. Do not bow to this. Do not accept it. It is wrong, and I will not stand by and watch you accept a wrong.

It was rebellion he was urging, open and armed, and he meant every word of it, and he had the strength to attempt it. The fire in him was real and dangerous. And here the two brothers stood face to face, the storm and the calm, and how Rāma met his brother’s rage is one of the great quiet scenes of the epic.

Rāma did not answer fire with fire. He did not rebuke Lakshmaṇa harshly, for he understood that the rage came from love, and love, even when it is mistaken, must be honoured. He put his hands on his brother, and he spoke to him gently, and he reasoned with him, cooling the fever in him not by opposing it but by drawing him up toward a higher view.

Peace, brother, he said. I know your anger, and I know it springs from your love for me, and I love you the more for it. But consider what you are truly urging. You would have me seize by force a throne that my father’s word has given elsewhere. You would have me set my own desire above his honour, break the sacred word of the house of Ikshvāku, and buy a crown with the coin of my father’s disgrace and perhaps his life. What would such a crown be worth, won so? A kingdom taken by trampling on my father’s truth and my duty as a son would be no kingdom but a theft, and I would be no king but a usurper who could not even keep faith with his own father. Where is the honour in that? You call the exile an injustice. Perhaps it is. But the answer to an injustice is not to commit a greater one. My father is bound by his word, and I am bound by my duty to him, and these bonds are not chains that shame me; they are the very things that make me who I am. Would you have me purchase fourteen years of comfort at the price of everything I hold sacred? I will not. And there is more, Lakshmaṇa: consider that perhaps this is not mere accident and intrigue at all, but the working-out of a destiny larger than we can see, a purpose that needs me in the forest and not on the throne, for reasons that will become clear in time. Do not fight the current of a river you cannot see the end of. Trust that this exile has its place in a design, and let us walk into it with open hearts rather than clenched fists.

And slowly, as Rāma spoke, the fire in Lakshmaṇa banked and cooled. He could not argue against his brother’s reasoning, for it was unanswerable; and more than that, the sheer serene certainty in Rāma reached the place in Lakshmaṇa that no argument could have reached, and quieted it. His rage, which had been ready to overturn a kingdom, subsided into something else, into the fierce devotion that would define the rest of his life. If Rāma would not be turned from the forest, then Lakshmaṇa knew what he himself would do, and it was the only thing he had ever really been going to do: he would go with him. He would not stay behind in comfort while his brother walked into the wild. Where Rāma went, Lakshmaṇa went; it had been true since they were children who could not sleep apart, and it was true now. His anger became resolve, and his resolve was to share the exile, to guard his brother through every one of the fourteen years, to be the sword and the shield and the tireless servant of Rāma’s forest life. The storm had passed into steady flame, and that flame would burn faithfully all the long years to come.

So in one morning the story showed three loves and three ways of grief: Kausalyā’s, which was sorrow, and had to be steadied into duty; Lakshmaṇa’s, which was fury, and had to be cooled into devotion; and above them both, Rāma’s own, which was neither sorrow nor fury but a great calm, the calm of a man who has surrendered everything except the one thing that matters, and holds that one thing so firmly that no storm can shake him. And by the strength of that calm he steadied his mother and quieted his brother and held the breaking house together, so that what might have become a palace revolt, a dynasty torn apart by armed rebellion, became instead an orderly and sorrowful preparation for a righteous man’s departure into the woods.

Sītā’s Resolve

There was one more heart to be told, and it was the heart nearest to his own. Rāma went to Sītā.

She did not yet know. She had spent the night, as he had, in the observances of one about to become the wife of a crowned prince, and she was waiting for him bright with expectation, ready to share the greatest day of their lives. And Rāma had to come to her and take that day away, and tell her that instead of a queen she was to be the wife of an exile, that instead of a palace her home for fourteen years would be the wilderness, and that he had come, in fact, to say goodbye, for he meant to go alone and leave her safe behind.

He told her gently, but he told her plainly, and then he told her his decision: that she must stay. The forest, he said, was no place for her. Let me describe to you what I go to, he said, so that you understand why I cannot take you. The Daṇḍaka is not a garden. It is a savage place, trackless and pathless, where the sun does not reach through the tangled canopy and the ground is a snarl of thorn and root. There are beasts there that hunt in the dark, tigers and wild elephants and serpents thick as a man’s thigh. There are demons, rākshasas, who devour the sages and defile the hermitages and would delight in the flesh of a princess. The food is roots and wild fruit; the bed is bare earth or heaped leaves; the rivers must be forded and the mountains climbed on foot; there is cold that bites to the bone and heat that flays, and rain that does not stop for weeks, and no comfort anywhere, and no safety, and no end to the hardship for fourteen long years. You were born in a palace and raised in one; your feet have known only marble and soft grass; how could I take you into that? It would break my heart to watch you suffer so. Stay here, he begged her, in comfort and in safety. Honour my parents in my absence. Wait for me. And I will come back to you.

He meant it as love, and it was love, but Sītā heard it and something rose in her that Rāma had perhaps not fully reckoned with, for beneath her gentleness Sītā had a will of iron, the same immovable strength that had lifted Shiva’s bow when she was a child, and it answered him now not with tears but with a fierce and dignified refusal that is one of the glories of the whole epic.

Why do you speak to me so, she asked him, as though I were a stranger, as though I were some fair-weather companion to be left behind when the weather turns? What is a wife? Is she an ornament for the good days only, to be set aside when hardship comes? Or is she half of her husband’s very self, bound to him not for the palace alone but for whatever the road brings, comfort or hardship, honour or exile, joy or grief? You describe to me the terrors of the forest as though they were arguments against my coming. They are the very reasons I must come. Do you imagine those dangers frighten me more than the thought of your facing them without me? Do you think I could sit here in safety and soft beds, eating from golden dishes, sleeping under a painted roof, while you, my life, my other self, walk barefoot through the thorns and sleep on the bare ground and face the beasts and the demons alone? That is not safety. That would be a torment beside which the worst the forest can offer is nothing.

And she went further, and her words cut to the root of the matter. Understand me, she said. For a wife who is a true wife, heaven itself would be a hell if her husband were not in it, and the harshest wilderness is a paradise if he is there. It is not the place that makes my happiness; it is you. Ayodhyā without you would be a desert, and the Daṇḍaka with you will be my home and my joy. The forest holds no terror for me that could equal the terror of being parted from you. Where you are, there is my palace; where you walk, there is my kingdom; your presence is my comfort and my safety and my whole desire. Do not speak to me of the hardships. I have weighed them, and they are nothing, they are less than nothing, beside the one thing I will not endure, which is to be left behind. Take me with you. It is my right as your wife, and it is my will, and I will not be moved.

Let us honour what Sītā is doing here, for it is easy to read it as mere devotion and it is far more than that. She is not passively clinging; she is asserting a truth about the nature of marriage and the nature of her own dignity. She is claiming her place, not begging for it. She is telling Rāma that to leave her behind would not be to protect her but to diminish her, to treat her as less than a full partner in his life and his dharma. Her love is not weakness but strength; her insistence is not desperation but a clear, reasoned, unshakable conviction about who she is and what she owes to the bond she has made. She has the same quality Rāma has, the quality of holding fast to a duty so deeply understood that no argument and no danger can shake it, and here that quality speaks in her, and it is magnificent.

Rāma heard her, and he could not answer her, because she was right, and because the strength in her matched the strength in him and recognized it. What could he say? He had urged her to safety out of love, and she had shown him that his love had almost led him to wound her, to deny her the very partnership that was the meaning of their marriage. He looked at her, this woman who would rather face demons at his side than sleep safe without him, and he understood that she was not a burden he was sparing but a strength he had nearly refused, and that the forest years would be immeasurably richer and warmer for her presence, and that to have left her would have been not kindness but a kind of poverty. He yielded, and gladly. She would come. Of course she would come. They would face the wilderness together, as they were meant to face everything together, and the exile that had seemed a desolation began, in that moment, to hold within it the seed of something that could not be taken from them: that whatever the fourteen years brought, they would meet it side by side.

And so it was settled that three would go into the forest and not one: Rāma, and Lakshmaṇa who would not be left, and Sītā who would not be left, the three of them bound each to the others by a love that had chosen hardship together over comfort apart. The palace that had prepared a coronation now prepared a departure, and the bark garments were brought, and the hour of leaving drew near.

To the Forest

The bark garments came. This was Kaikeyī’s doing too, one last cruelty pressed to its limit: she herself brought the rough valkala, the garments of woven bark that ascetics wear, and pressed them upon the three who were to go, so that they should leave not in the silks of royalty but in the coarse dress of hermits from the very first hour. Rāma took his without a word and put it on, and Lakshmaṇa his, and the two princes stood transformed, their royal ornaments laid aside, clad like forest-dwellers.

But when Kaikeyī moved to clothe Sītā too in bark, the old ministers and the elders of the court could not bear it, and there was an outcry. It was one thing, they said, to exile the prince by the letter of a rash oath; it was another to strip a princess, a daughter of a royal house who had done no wrong and against whom no boon had been claimed, of her very garments. Even the broken king roused himself enough to spare her that. So Sītā went in her own clothes, at least, though she went; and the sight of the delicate princess preparing to walk into the wilderness wrung the whole court with grief.

And then the leaving itself, and here the story opens out from the private chamber to the whole vast public sorrow of a city losing the thing it loved most.

For Ayodhyā had learned what had happened, and Ayodhyā was in agony. The city that had blazed with lamps two nights before, certain of its happy morning, now understood that its prince, the man it had loved past all reason and longed to see crowned, was instead being driven into the forest by a stepmother’s spite and an old king’s rash word. And the people would not bear it in silence. They poured into the streets. They gathered along the ceremonial way that the chariot must take, and they wept, and they cried out, and their grief was a living thing that filled the whole capital.

Sumantra, the faithful old charioteer and minister, brought the chariot, for the king had commanded at least that his son be conveyed with honour to the border of the kingdom before being set down to walk. The three climbed in, Rāma and Sītā and Lakshmaṇa, in their hermit dress, and Sumantra took up the reins, and the chariot began to move through the grieving city toward the gate.

And the people would not let it go. They ran alongside. They pressed against the wheels. They clung to the chariot, to its sides, to its very axles, trying by the sheer force of their love and their bodies to slow it, to stop it, to keep Rāma among them a little longer. Do not go, they cried. Do not leave us. If Rāma must live in the forest, then let the forest be here, let us all go with him, let Ayodhyā itself be emptied and follow him into the wild, for a city without Rāma is no city, only walls and dust. They begged Sumantra to drive slowly, slowly, and he did, weeping himself, hardly able to see the road; and the great crowd moved with the chariot like a single grieving creature, and the sound of the city’s weeping rose up and filled the sky.

Think of what this crowd was. It was not the grief of courtiers who had lost a patron, nor of soldiers who had lost a commander. It was the grief of ordinary people, the merchants and the labourers and the poor, who had lost the one great man who had truly seen them, who remembered their names and their troubles, who had made them feel that the throne itself cared whether they lived or died. They were not mourning a prince in the abstract. They were mourning a man each of them felt he had lost personally, and their grief was the truest measure of what kind of ruler Ayodhyā was losing, for the love of the common people, freely given, is a thing no king can command and no gold can buy, and Rāma had it wholly, and it was following him out the gate in a great weeping tide.

And behind them, in the palace, the old king could bear it no longer. Dasharatha, who had lain broken through the long night, dragged himself up when he understood that the chariot was actually leaving, that his son was actually going, and he came stumbling out into the open, out of the palace, into the street, an old king unkinged by grief, crying out his son’s name. Rāma, he called, Rāma, wait, stop, do not go, come back to me. He staggered after the chariot, this ancient man who had ruled a golden age and fought beside the gods, running now on failing legs through the public street, weeping, calling his son’s name to a chariot that was already too far ahead, already lost in the crowd and the dust.

But Rāma had given Sumantra a quiet instruction, and it was a hard one, and it was mercy disguised as cruelty. Drive on, he had said. Do not stop. For if we stop, if I turn back, if I go to my father, the parting will only have to be made again, and each making of it will be a fresh wound, and my father’s grief and the city’s grief will only be prolonged and deepened. A clean cut heals better than a ragged one. Drive on, Sumantra, and let the leaving be swift, for their sakes as much as ours. And so, though it tore his own heart, Rāma did not stop the chariot for his weeping father, but had it driven on, faster now, out through the great gate and away, leaving the old king behind in the road.

And there the tellers leave Dasharatha for the moment, and it is an image that has never left the memory of those who love this story: the great king collapsed in the public dust of his own capital, stretching out his arms toward the vanishing chariot, crying his son’s name to the empty road, abandoned by his own oath, undone by his own honour, watching the dearest thing in his life disappear into the distance and knowing, in his bones, that he would never see it again. For that was the truth that broke him past all mending, and he was right in it: he would not live to see Rāma return. The parting in the road was the last he would ever have.

The chariot passed out of the city and into the countryside, and behind it, for a long way, the people still followed, unwilling to turn back, walking after their prince into the gathering evening because they could not bear to let him go. And Rāma, looking back at them, at the great faithful weeping crowd that had left its homes to follow him, was moved as perhaps nothing else had moved him that whole terrible day, and he resolved to do for them the one kindness left to him: to slip away from them, so that they might be freed to return to their lives. But that belongs to the next stage of the road, to the river Tamasā and the first night of the exile, and to the quiet, sorrowful cunning by which Rāma at last released his people to go home.

Alone by Themselves

They came at dusk to the banks of the river Tamasā, and there they halted for the first night of the exile, and the great crowd of citizens halted with them, camping along the river, unwilling still to let their prince out of their sight. And Rāma, watching them settle for the night around him, understood that they would follow him forever if he let them, all the way into the wilderness, ruining their own lives out of love for him, and he understood that the kindest thing he could do was to leave them, and that they would never consent to be left. So he chose a gentle deception, the only kind of deception a man like Rāma ever practised, one meant wholly for the good of those it deceived.

In the deep of the night, while the exhausted citizens slept, worn out with the day’s grief and the long walk, Rāma quietly woke Sumantra and had the chariot readied in silence, and the three of them slipped away in the dark, going on ahead while the people slept, and taking care that the chariot’s tracks should be confused so that the citizens could not easily follow. When the people woke at dawn and found the place empty, found that Rāma had gone on without them in the night, they understood at last what he had done and why, and they grieved afresh, but they understood too that he had released them out of love, that he did not wish them to destroy themselves for his sake, and slowly, sorrowfully, having no choice now, they turned back toward Ayodhyā, carrying their grief home with them. It was the only way. He could not have argued them into leaving; he could only slip free while they slept and let the accomplished fact turn them homeward.

Now the three went on alone, and truly alone for the first time, and the world changed character around them. They came to the Gangā, the great and holy river, the broad shining boundary between the settled kingdom and the wild lands beyond, and here they met a man who mattered.

His name was Guha, and he was the chief of the Nishādas, the tribe of hunters and boatmen who lived along the river. He was not a man of the cities or the courts; he was a forest chieftain, a hunter, a man some at Ayodhyā would have thought beneath their notice. But he loved Rāma, for Rāma’s fame had reached even the river-tribes, and when he learned that the prince himself had come to his shore, in exile, in bark garments, he came out to meet him with his whole heart.

And here the story shows us something about Rāma that it wants us to see clearly. Guha received Rāma not with the distant respect a tribesman might be expected to show a prince, but with the open love of a friend, and Rāma returned it in exactly the same coin. He embraced Guha as a brother. He did not stand on rank; he did not hold the hunter-chief at the arm’s length that his birth might have licensed; he met Guha’s love with love, plainly and warmly, as an equal. This is not a small thing. It is one of the deep marks of Rāma’s greatness that his goodness knew nothing of caste or station, that he saw the soul of a man and not his rank, and that a forest hunter who loved him truly was dearer to him than any high-born flatterer. The love that the common people of Ayodhyā had borne him, and that had followed him weeping to the Tamasā, was of a piece with this: Rāma was loved by the humble because Rāma genuinely loved the humble, and here on the riverbank that truth stood plainly revealed.

Guha, overwhelmed to have Rāma on his shore, offered him everything he had. Stay here, he begged. Do not go on into the terrible forest. Rule here, among my people; my whole territory is yours; my hunters are your servants; live here in what comfort the river-country can offer, and let me serve you all your days. He offered his kingdom, such as it was, with the same open generosity that a great king might have offered an empire, and it was worth as much, for it was everything he had.

And Rāma declined it, gently, with love, and his reason is important. I cannot, dear friend, he said. Not because I do not honour your gift, for I honour it above many a richer one, offered as it is with such a pure heart. But my father’s word sent me to live as an ascetic in the forest for fourteen years, and to accept your hospitality, to live here in comfort and rule, would be to evade that word, to keep its letter while betraying its spirit. I did not come into exile to find a softer exile. I came to live the hard forest life my father’s vow requires, and I must live it truly, or my acceptance of it is a sham. Your love I keep and treasure; your kingdom I cannot take; for the whole meaning of my going is that I go to hardship, and I will not soften what I have undertaken. It was the same principle that had governed everything since the dark chamber: that duty half-done is duty betrayed, and that the value of a sacrifice lies precisely in not evading its cost.

There was one thing, though, that had to be done before they crossed, and it is a small quiet moment that the tellers love. Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, to complete their transformation into forest ascetics, needed to mat their hair as the hermits did, and for this they used the sap of the banyan tree, the milky sap that would bind and knot the hair into the ascetic’s matted locks. Guha brought it, and the brothers matted their hair, and with that the change was complete: the two princes of Ayodhyā, who two mornings before had been dressed for a coronation, now stood on the riverbank with matted hair and bark garments, indistinguishable from the forest hermits they had become. Something in the finality of that small act, the royal hair bound up into the ascetic’s knots, brought home the completeness of what they had given up, and it is said that even Lakshmaṇa’s steadiness wavered at the sight, and that Guha wept openly.

Then Guha ferried them across. He brought his own boat, and with his own hands he rowed the prince he loved across the wide Gangā, from the settled world into the wild, and it was the last service the world of men would do for them for a long time. They stepped out on the far bank, the three of them, into the true forest at last, and Guha stood in his boat on the water and watched them go, watched the three figures walk away from the river and toward the trees, growing smaller, until at last they passed in among the dark woods that led toward Chitrakūṭa and were lost to his sight. And he stayed there a long while, the hunter-chief, looking at the place where they had vanished, before he turned his boat and rowed slowly back to a shore that felt emptier than it had ever felt before.

They were alone now, truly and finally alone, three figures walking into a green wilderness, the kingdom behind them, the fourteen years ahead of them, the whole vast forest closing over them like water over a stone. Whatever comfort the world of men could give was on the far side of the river now. From here the road ran only into the wild.

Chitrakūṭa

Beyond the Gangā the land grew wilder, but not, at first, more terrible. They walked on, the three of them, deeper into the forest, and along the way they came to the hermitage of a great sage, Bharadvāja, whose ashram stood where the rivers met, and there they were received with the grave sweet hospitality that the forest sages always showed to Rāma, for holiness knows holiness, and the hermits of the wilderness understood, as the schemers of the palace had not, who it was that walked among them.

Bharadvāja welcomed them, and fed them, and when Rāma asked the sage where they might settle to pass the years of exile, the old man had an answer ready, and it was a gift. Go to Chitrakūṭa, he told them. There is a hill there, and a river below it, the Mandākinī, and it is among the most beautiful and peaceful places in all the wide forest. The air is sweet there; the sages love it; the beasts are gentle and the birds are many; the very sight of the hill lifts the heart and quiets sorrow. Make your home there, and the years will pass more kindly than you fear.

So they went on to Chitrakūṭa, and found it everything the sage had promised.

Let us dwell here a while, as they did, because after the darkness of the preceding days the story pauses to breathe, and we should breathe with it. Chitrakūṭa was beautiful. The hill rose green and wooded above the plain, and the Mandākinī ran clear and cool at its foot, and the whole place had a serene loveliness that seemed to belong to an easier and older world. There were flowering trees whose blossoms scented the air. There were birds of every colour, peacocks that spread their trains in the mornings and cuckoos that called from the shade, and deer that came down to the water without fear and lifted their heads to watch the newcomers with mild curious eyes. There were clear pools where lotuses opened, and slopes of soft grass, and views from the higher rocks out over an endless green world. It was the kind of place where a heart bruised by the world might slowly heal, and it worked that healing on the three of them, so that the exile, which had begun in so much grief, took on here for a while the character almost of a blessing.

And they made a home. This is one of the tender pleasures of this part of the story, to watch these three, who had left a palace, build for themselves with their own hands a small dwelling in the wild, and find in the doing of it a happiness the palace had never given them. Lakshmaṇa took the labour of it upon himself, for that was his joy, to serve, to do the hard and useful work that made his brother’s life easier. He it was who chose the site and cleared it, who cut and gathered the timber and the reeds, who raised the framework and thatched the roof and packed the walls, building with tireless devotion a cottage of leaf and mud and wood, snug and sound, a real home in the heart of the forest. He worked at it as though it were the most important commission of his life, and in a way it was, for it was the house his brother and his sister-in- law would live in, and he built it with all the love that was in him.

We should notice what Lakshmaṇa is, in these forest years, for it is easy to overlook the quiet ones. He was a prince, a warrior of tremendous power, a man who might have stayed in Ayodhyā in comfort and honour; and he had thrown all of that away, without a second thought, to come and be, in effect, the servant of his brother’s exile. He cut the wood and carried the water and stood the night watches and built the house and cooked the food and asked for nothing, and he did it not with the resentment of a man who has stooped but with the gladness of a man who has found his whole purpose. There is a kind of greatness in that willing lowering of oneself, in the choice to serve where one might have ruled, and Lakshmaṇa had it, and the forest years are his long quiet glory as much as they are anyone’s. The devotion that had begun in the cradle, the child who would not sleep apart from his brother, had grown into this: a man who would not let his brother suffer the hardships of exile alone, and who took the heaviest share of them cheerfully upon himself.

And so, in the cottage that Lakshmaṇa built, on the beautiful hill above the clear river, the three of them settled into a life. And it was, for a while, a good life, better in some ways than the life they had left. The days had a simple shape: the gathering of fruit and roots, the fetching of water, the tending of the small sacred fire, the long evenings of talk, the nights under a roof of leaves with the river singing below and the enormous star-crowded forest dark all around. There was no court, no intrigue, no ceremony, no crowd of petitioners and flatterers, only the three of them and the mountain and the river and the gentle wild creatures. Rāma, who bore his losses so lightly because he held so firmly to the one thing that mattered, was able here to be almost purely happy, and Sītā beside him was happy, and Lakshmaṇa serving them both was happy, and for a season the exile was not a punishment but a kind of retreat, a stripping-away of everything unnecessary until only the essential remained: love, and simplicity, and peace.

It could not last. We know it could not last, and the story knows it, and there is a poignancy in the very beauty of Chitrakūṭa because we understand, as the three of them settling so contentedly did not yet fully understand, that this peace was an island in a rising flood, that the world they had left was already convulsing with the consequences of what had been done, and that the calm of the green hill was bought on borrowed time. Even now, far to the north, in the city they had left, grief was doing its work, and a death was coming, and after the death an army would come south looking for them, and the peace of Chitrakūṭa would be broken. But that had not happened yet. For now there was only the beautiful hill, and the clear river, and the cottage of leaves, and three people who loved one another living simply and gladly in the heart of the wild, and it is right to let that picture stand in its full sweetness, because there will not be many more like it, and because the very happiness of it is part of what the story means us to feel, so that we understand, when the peace breaks, exactly what is being broken.

A Mother’s Grief

While the three found their fragile peace at Chitrakūṭa, Ayodhyā was a house of mourning, and at the centre of the mourning were two broken people: an old queen who had lost her son, and an old king who had lost everything and was dying of it.

Kausalyā’s grief was the grief of a mother, and it had a particular bitterness in it, for she had waited so long and been passed over so often. She was the senior queen, the first wife, and yet through all the years it had been Kaikeyī who held the king’s heart, Kaikeyī who was cherished and indulged, while Kausalyā kept her dignity and her patience and her place. Her one consolation, her one great joy, the thing that made all the quiet years of being the less-loved wife worthwhile, was her son. Rāma was everything to her. And the day of his coronation was to have been her vindication, the day when her patience was crowned along with her boy, when she would at last take her rightful place as the mother of the king. And that day had been snatched away and turned into this: her son in the wilderness, her rival’s son on the path to the throne, and herself left alone in a palace that had become a place of ashes.

She wept, and she could not stop weeping. She railed against Kaikeyī, against the king, against the fate that had done this to her. She lay in her chambers and would not be comforted, and the sight of her grief was terrible to those who loved her.

And into that grief came Sumitrā, and here the story gives us a portrait worth pausing on, for Sumitrā is one of its quiet wise women, easy to overlook and deeply admirable. Sumitrā was the third queen, the mother of Lakshmaṇa and Shatrughna, and she had lost a son to the forest too, for her Lakshmaṇa had gone with Rāma. She had as much cause to grieve as Kausalyā. But Sumitrā met the catastrophe with a strength and a wisdom that lifted everyone around her, and instead of drowning in her own sorrow she gave herself to steadying Kausalyā’s.

Do not grieve so, sister, she said, or words to that effect, and her comfort was not the empty comfort of one who does not understand, for she understood completely; it was the true comfort of one who sees further into the situation than grief can see. Consider who your son is, she told Kausalyā. Consider what manner of being Rāma is. Do you truly fear for him in the forest? The forest should fear him. He whom the demons flee, he who broke the bow of Shiva, he who is guarded by his own dharma and by Lakshmaṇa’s tireless bow, what harm can the wilderness do to such a one? And consider Sītā, who chose to follow him, and my Lakshmaṇa, who guards him night and day. They are together, the three of them, and they are strong, and they are righteous, and the righteous are not finally abandoned by heaven. This exile is a hardship, yes, but it is not a doom. Fourteen years will pass. And when they pass, your son will return, not diminished but glorified, tempered by his trials, beloved more than ever, and he will be crowned after all, and you will take your place as the mother of the king, and this grief will be a memory, a dark passage that led to a bright morning. Weep if you must, but do not despair, for despair would be an insult to the greatness of your son and the justice of the powers that watch over him.

And by such words, Sumitrā slowly drew Kausalyā up out of the worst of her grief, not by denying the sorrow but by setting it in a larger frame, by reminding the grieving mother that her son was no ordinary man cast helpless into danger, but a being whom the danger could not touch, walking a road that led, however darkly, toward a return. It is the gift of the truly wise in a time of catastrophe, that they can hold the long view when everyone around them can see only the immediate wound, and Sumitrā had that gift, and she used it to save Kausalyā from being destroyed by her own sorrow.

We might pause on the difference between these two women, for the story clearly wants us to see it. Both had lost a son to the forest. Kausalyā met it with a grief that turned inward, that railed and despaired and could see nothing beyond its own wound. Sumitrā met it with a grief mastered by faith and wisdom, a grief that could still look up and out, that could comfort another even while carrying its own loss. Neither loved her son less than the other. But Sumitrā had something Kausalyā in her first grief had lost, a trust in the larger order of things, a confidence that the righteous are not finally forsaken, and that trust gave her a strength that grief could not overthrow. It is a thing worth wanting for ourselves, that steadiness that can grieve without despairing, that can feel the full weight of a loss and still keep faith that the loss is not the end of the story.

But if Kausalyā could be lifted out of her grief, there was one in that palace who could not be lifted out of his, and whose grief was not merely sorrow but a mortal sickness. Dasharatha was dying. From the moment the chariot had passed out of sight, taking his son, the old king had begun to fail. He had no wish to live in a world without Rāma, and more than that, he was crushed by the knowledge of his own part in the catastrophe, that it was his rash boons, his own honoured word, that had driven his son away. He could not eat. He could not sleep. He lay in his chambers growing weaker by the day, calling Rāma’s name, reliving the parting, sinking steadily toward an end that everyone around him could see coming and no one could prevent.

And there was something more that haunted his dying, a thing from his own distant past that had risen up now to claim him, a memory of a sin committed long ago in his youth, and a curse that had been laid upon him then, whose hour, he now understood with dreadful clarity, had come round at last. For Dasharatha’s death was not a simple death of grief. It was the closing of a circle begun long before Rāma was born, the falling due of an old debt, and to understand why the old king died as he died, we must go back with him, as he went back in his last hours, to a night on the banks of the Sarayū many years before, and to the terrible thing he did there, and the curse it earned him.

Idle Sport and Terrible Result

In his last hours, as the strength ebbed from him, Dasharatha called Kausalyā to his side, and in the darkness he told her a thing he had carried secret for the whole of his long life, a thing he had done in his youth, and the curse it had earned him, and why he now understood that his death from grief for his son was no accident but the exact and just fruit of that ancient deed. Listen, he said, for I must tell this before I die, so that you understand that what is happening to me is justice, and that I have earned it, and that I do not die wronged but repaid.

When he was young, he told her, long before he was old, before he had sons, before he had even wed his queens, he had been a keen hunter, and proud of a particular skill. He could shoot by sound alone. In the dark, or through cover, guided only by his ears, he could send an arrow unerringly toward any sound of a creature moving, and strike it dead without ever seeing it. He was vain of this skill, as young men are vain of their talents, and he practised it as a sport, this killing of unseen things by the sound they made.

One evening he had gone down to the banks of the Sarayū to hunt in this fashion, waiting in the dusk by the water for the animals that came down to drink. And as he waited, he heard a sound from the water’s edge, a gurgling, bubbling sound, exactly the sound, he was certain, of an elephant filling its trunk to drink. It was just the kind of target his sport delighted in, a creature betraying itself by sound in the failing light. Without hesitation, without seeing, guided only by his ear, he drew and loosed his arrow straight at the sound.

And a human voice cried out.

The cry that came back to him across the darkening water was not the trumpet of a stricken elephant but the scream of a wounded boy, a young human voice raised in agony and astonishment, crying out that he had been struck, that he was dying, and asking, in his pain, who had done this thing and why, what wrong had he ever done to earn an arrow in the dark.

Dasharatha’s blood froze. He ran to the sound, and there at the water’s edge he found not an animal but a young man, an ascetic youth, a boy who had come down to the river in the dusk to fill a water-jar for his aged parents, and the gurgling of the jar filling had been the sound Dasharatha’s arrow had flown to. The boy lay in the shallows with the shaft in him, his life running out into the river, and he looked up at the horrified king with no hatred, only a terrible sorrow, and spoke.

His name, he said, was Shravaṇa. He was the only son of an old couple who lived in a hermitage nearby, and his parents were both blind, and utterly dependent on him, for he was their eyes and their hands and their only support in the world. He had come to fetch them water. And now he was dying, and his last and only thought was not for himself but for them: who would care for his blind old parents now? Who would bring them water, and food, and guide their steps? He had been their whole world, and he was being torn out of it by a stranger’s careless arrow, and they did not even know. Draw out the arrow, he asked the king at last, for it pains me, though it will kill me to draw it; and then go to my parents, and tell them what has happened, and care for them if you have any goodness in you, for they cannot live alone.

We must feel the full horror of this, as Dasharatha felt it, for it is one of the darkest moments in his whole long life. He had killed an innocent. Not in war, not in defence, not in any righteous cause, but in idle sport, shooting at a sound in the dark for the vain pleasure of his own skill, and the sound had been a good and gentle boy fetching water for his blind parents.
